_meta.description: Curated wellness SNP lookup table for DNA raw data import. Forward (+) strand alleles. Evidence strength and personal relevance are graded separately; legacy effect fields remain for compatibility and are not scientific evidence grades. snpHints connect genetics to supplement recommendation slots.

evidenceFramework.reviewScope: All retained links were checked for claim relevance at metadata and abstract level; full text or supporting tables were reviewed for targeted ambiguous or high-impact claims. This is not a systematic full-text review of every publication.

rs671.strandNote: dbSNP forward: G(ref Glu504) / A(alt Lys504 = ALDH2*2). 0% in Europeans/Africans; ~28–45% allele frequency in East Asians — one of the most population-stratified clinically relevant SNPs.

evidence.scope: Established ALDH2 loss of function and alcohol-dependent acetaldehyde effects; health-risk estimates are exposure- and ancestry-dependent.

relevance.context: Alcohol exposure determines whether the health-risk association is expressed.

GG.note: Normal ALDH2; standard acetaldehyde clearance

GA.note: One dysfunctional, dominant-negative ALDH2*2 allele; facial flushing and lower alcohol tolerance. Drinking substantially amplifies esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma risk in carriers.

AA.note: Two ALDH2*2 alleles; very low acetaldehyde clearance, usually causing severe flushing and nausea with alcohol. Avoiding alcohol also avoids the acetaldehyde exposure implicated in cancer risk.

GA.text: Your ALDH2 Glu504Lys (heterozygous) slows acetaldehyde clearance. Limiting or avoiding alcohol reduces the exposure linked to esophageal-cancer risk in ALDH2*2 carriers.

AA.text: Your ALDH2 Glu504Lys (homozygous) indicates very low acetaldehyde clearance. Avoiding alcohol is the direct way to avoid this exposure.

rs5882.strandNote: dbSNP forward: A(ref Ile) / G(alt Val). G ≈ 0.32 globally. Complements existing rs708272 TaqIB (partially correlated, r² ≈ 0.5 in CEU — not redundant).

evidence.scope: HDL associations appear in some cohorts, while cardiovascular and longevity directions vary across populations.

relevance.context: A lipid panel is more informative than this genotype, and no genotype-specific action follows.

AA.note: Ile/Ile reference genotype. Reported HDL, cardiovascular, and longevity associations vary across cohorts and ancestry groups.

AG.note: Ile/Val genotype. Some cohorts report higher HDL with the Val allele, but clinical associations are not consistent across populations.

GG.note: Val/Val was associated with higher HDL and lower myocardial-infarction risk in men in the Rotterdam cohort. Longevity findings vary by ancestry and are not consistently protective.

rs6257.strandNote: Forward strand: T (major) / C (minor). In the cited cohorts, C carriers had modestly lower SHBG than TT, but this was not replicated in every population and does not predict a person's hormone status by itself.

evidence.scope: A modest SHBG association was observed in two cohorts but was not reproduced in another population.

relevance.context: Use a measured hormone panel rather than this SNP to assess current hormone status.

CC.note: C/C is the minor-allele genotype. C carriers had about 10% lower SHBG than TT in two prospective cohorts; another cohort did not find a significant rs6257 effect. A blood measurement is more informative than this SNP.

CT.note: C/T carriers had modestly lower SHBG than TT in two prospective cohorts, but the association was not consistent in every population.

TT.note: T/T is the major comparison genotype and was associated with somewhat higher SHBG than C-carrier genotypes in two cohorts.

evidence.scope: This is one of two well-established APOE-defining markers and has no standalone haplotype interpretation.

relevance.context: Interpret only as the rs429358/rs7412 APOE haplotype and with broader health and family context.

CC.note: APOE part 2 — combine with rs429358 for haplotype

CT.note: APOE part 2 — one ε2 allele possible

TT.note: APOE part 2 — ε2/ε2 possible

rs174546.markerNote: FADS-cluster tag associated with estimated delta-5 desaturase activity and n-6 fatty-acid profiles; maps to the omega-3 index for measured context.
rs174546.strandNote: Forward strand: C/T. In the cited European cohort, each T allele tracked with lower estimated delta-5 desaturase activity. The study was observational and did not test omega-3 supplementation.

evidence.scope: A human cohort supports an association with estimated desaturase activity and fatty-acid profiles, not supplement response.

relevance.context: Measured fatty-acid status is needed before drawing dietary or supplement conclusions.

CC.note: C/C was the higher estimated delta-5 desaturase-activity comparison genotype in the cited European cohort.

TC.note: One T allele was associated with lower estimated delta-5 desaturase activity and altered n-6 fatty-acid profiles.

TT.note: Two T alleles were associated with lower estimated delta-5 desaturase activity and altered n-6 fatty-acid profiles; this does not by itself establish poor omega-3 conversion or a supplement need.

TC.text: Your FADS1 rs174546 genotype is associated with lower estimated desaturase activity; your measured omega-3 index can show whether food or supplement changes improve your actual status.

TT.text: Your FADS1 rs174546 genotype is associated with lower estimated desaturase activity; use your measured omega-3 index rather than the genotype alone to evaluate diet or supplements.

rs174547.markerNote: In strong linkage disequilibrium with rs174546; largely redundant as an independent signal.
rs174547.strandNote: Forward strand: T/C. In the cited study, C carriers had lower estimated desaturase activity than T carriers in both young Caucasian and Asian groups, although which allele was less common differed between the groups.

evidence.scope: A small multi-ancestry human study supports an estimated desaturase-activity association at a correlated FADS marker.

relevance.context: This linked marker is biochemical context and does not establish a deficiency or intervention need.

CC.note: C carriers had lower estimated delta-5 desaturase activity than T carriers in the cited small multi-ancestry study.

TC.note: C/T was associated with lower estimated delta-5 desaturase activity than T/T; this marker is strongly correlated with nearby FADS variants.

TT.note: T/T was the higher estimated desaturase-activity comparison genotype in the cited study.

rs174575.markerNote: Maps to custom fatty acid markers (GLA, AA, EPA, DHA)

evidence.scope: The catalog claim comes from a small pregnancy cohort and may not generalize beyond that population or setting.

relevance.context: Treat as fatty-acid trait context rather than a diagnosis or supplement indication.

CC.note: Reference genotype. In a small pregnancy cohort, maternal fatty-acid levels varied by rs174575 genotype.

CG.note: Heterozygous genotype; the cited cohort reported genotype-related differences in long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, not a diagnosed enzyme deficiency.

GG.note: Associated with lower arachidonic acid, EPA, and DHA in breast milk in a small cohort of pregnant women; applicability outside that setting is uncertain.

evidence.scope: A common-variant Graves disease association is supported, but it is not diagnostic and does not apply to Hashimoto disease.

relevance.context: Symptoms, thyroid testing, antibodies, and family history matter more than this common SNP alone.

GG.note: Low Graves' disease risk

AA.note: Significantly elevated Graves' disease risk (~2-3×); no association with Hashimoto's

rs225014.strandNote: Forward strand: T(ref Thr92) / C(alt Ala92). Evidence is mixed: mechanistic studies report altered DIO2 behavior, while a large population cohort found no material association with thyroid parameters, quality of life, or cognition.

evidence.scope: Mechanistic and thyroid-tissue findings have not translated into a consistent population phenotype or treatment response.

relevance.context: No genotype-specific thyroid treatment follows from this marker.

TT.note: Thr/Thr reference genotype. A large cohort found no material genotype association with thyroid parameters or quality-of-life measures.

TC.note: Thr/Ala genotype. Laboratory and thyroidectomy studies suggest altered DIO2 function, but large population data did not show a clear clinical effect.

CC.note: Ala/Ala genotype. Mechanistic and thyroidectomy evidence suggests reduced local T4-to-T3 conversion, but this has not translated into a consistent population-level clinical phenotype or a genotype-specific treatment recommendation.

evidence.scope: Evidence for a directional common-variant effect on CBS activity or homocysteine is limited and debated.

relevance.context: Homocysteine and relevant nutrient markers are more informative than this genotype.

GG.note: Normal transsulfuration pathway activity

GA.note: Altered CBS activity; clinical significance debated

AA.note: Altered CBS activity; may affect homocysteine clearance (direction uncertain)

GA.text: Your CBS c.699C>T genotype is a modest, context-dependent association marker; use measured homocysteine and nutritional status rather than this SNP alone to decide on B6.

AA.text: Your CBS c.699C>T genotype is a modest, context-dependent association marker; check homocysteine and nutritional status before inferring a B6 need.

evidence.scope: This is one of two well-established APOE-defining markers and has no standalone haplotype interpretation.

relevance.context: Interpret only as the rs429358/rs7412 APOE haplotype and with broader health and family context.

TT.note: APOE part 1 — combine with rs7412 for haplotype

TC.note: APOE part 1 — one ε4 allele possible

CC.note: APOE part 1 — ε4/ε4 possible

evidence.scope: Human association evidence supports lower total B12 through haptocorrin, with less certain relevance to active B12 status.

relevance.context: Interpret with holotranscobalamin, MMA, homocysteine, and diet rather than serum B12 alone.

AA.note: Normal haptocorrin production

GG.note: Lower haptocorrin; lower total serum B12 (holoTC may be less affected)

evidence.scope: FUT2 secretor status is functional and associated with B12-related biomarkers, but serum B12 direction can be misleading.

relevance.context: Functional B12 markers are needed because non-secretor status can alter total serum B12 without proving better status.

GG.note: Secretor (wild-type); normal gut microbiome composition and intrinsic-factor B12 uptake

GA.note: Heterozygous secretor; intermediate B12 levels, typically clinically unremarkable

AA.note: Non-secretor; higher total B12 (lab artifact from haptocorrin); does not indicate better B12 status — check functional markers (homocysteine, MMA) rather than trusting serum B12

GA.text: Your FUT2 W154X genotype can affect the interpretation of total B12; use functional markers such as methylmalonic acid or homocysteine rather than preferring one B12 form from genotype alone.

rs700518.strandNote: Forward strand: C(ref)/T(alt) — actual Ancestry alleles. Literature cites A/G (complement).

evidence.scope: Published hormone findings concern CYP19A1 haplotypes and do not support a reliable standalone direction for rs700518.

relevance.context: Do not infer aromatase activity or hormone status from this SNP alone.

CC.note: Reference genotype. The cited study found hormone associations for CYP19A1 haplotypes rather than a reliable standalone effect for rs700518.

CT.note: Heterozygous genotype; any hormone association appears context- and haplotype-dependent.

TT.note: Alternate homozygous genotype; rs700518 alone does not establish a direction of aromatase activity or hormone conversion.

rs708272.strandNote: dbSNP forward alleles G/A (= classical B2/B1). Old literature uses G/T (reverse strand) — A allele here is the same as the T allele in older papers.

evidence.scope: The cited cohort supports an HDL association but not a genotype-specific myocardial-infarction difference.

relevance.context: Use measured lipids and overall cardiovascular context; this marker does not establish protection.

GG.note: B2/B2 was associated with higher HDL in the cited cohort, but not with a lower myocardial-infarction rate.

GA.note: B1/B2 genotype; HDL was intermediate in the cited cohort, without evidence of a genotype-specific reduction in myocardial infarction.

AA.note: B1/B1 genotype; associated with lower HDL than B2/B2 in the cited cohort, but myocardial-infarction rates did not differ by genotype.

rs743572.strandNote: Forward strand: A(ref)/G(alt). Literature often cites T/C (complement).

evidence.scope: A large human study did not support a reliable circulating-hormone or prostate-cancer association for this SNP.

relevance.context: No steroid-production or health conclusion should be inferred from this marker.

AA.note: Reference genotype. A large study found no association between rs743572 and circulating sex hormones or prostate-cancer risk.

AG.note: Heterozygous genotype; the cited large study did not find a measurable circulating-hormone difference.

GG.note: Alternate homozygous genotype; current evidence does not support inferring higher steroid synthesis from this SNP alone.

rs762551.strandNote: dbSNP forward: A(ref, fast inducible) / C(alt, slow). 23andMe / Ancestry / Illumina report A/C. C ≈ 0.32 globally, fairly even across populations.

evidence.scope: CYP1A2 inducibility and caffeine metabolism are supported; the cardiovascular interaction comes from exposure-specific observational evidence.

relevance.context: Caffeine amount, timing, smoking, medications, and symptoms materially change its meaning.

AA.note: Fast metabolizer (*1F/*1F); rapid caffeine clearance; strongly inducible by smoking and cruciferous vegetables

AC.note: Intermediate metabolizer; caffeine cleared at moderate rate

CC.note: Slow metabolizer; in the cited case-control study, coffee intake was associated with higher non-fatal myocardial-infarction risk among C-allele carriers, especially at four or more cups per day.

AC.text: Your CYP1A2 *1F genotype includes the slower-metabolizing C allele. The cited study supports being cautious with high coffee intake, particularly four or more cups per day.

CC.text: Your CYP1A2 *1F genotype is the slower-metabolizing CC form. The cited study supports limiting high coffee intake rather than predicting an exact clearance time.

rs855791.strandNote: Forward strand: G(ref=Ala736)/A(alt=Val736). Literature often cites T/C (complement).

evidence.scope: Replicated human genetic and functional evidence links this TMPRSS6 variant to hepcidin and iron-status differences.

relevance.context: Ferritin, transferrin saturation, CBC, diet, and blood loss determine current iron status.

AA.note: Higher hepcidin → lower iron absorption; risk of iron-deficiency anemia

GG.note: Efficient hepcidin suppression; normal iron absorption

AA.text: Your TMPRSS6 V736A genotype is associated with lower hemoglobin and iron measures in population studies; check ferritin, transferrin saturation, and blood count before considering iron.

AG.text: Your TMPRSS6 V736A genotype has a modest association with iron-related measures; use ferritin, transferrin saturation, and blood count rather than genotype alone to decide on iron.

rs953413.markerNote: Maps to custom fatty acid markers (EPA, DHA, Omega-3 Index)

evidence.scope: Human response data and enhancer experiments support ELOVL2 expression and fatty-acid associations without proving deficiency.

relevance.context: Measured fatty acids and diet are needed to interpret any practical relevance.

AA.note: A/A genotype. The mechanistic study found lower enhancer activity than with the G allele; fatty-acid levels and fish-oil response still depend on more than this SNP.

AG.note: A/G genotype. rs953413 was associated with differences in ELOVL2 expression and with fatty-acid response to fish-oil supplementation, without establishing a simple deficiency state.

GG.note: G/G genotype. The G allele increases enhancer binding and ELOVL2 expression in the mechanistic study; it should not be interpreted as reduced elongase activity.

evidence.scope: Laboratory evidence supports altered CYP1B1 catalytic activity, but the catalog does not establish a reliable personal health outcome.

relevance.context: Treat as enzyme-function context, not as a hormone diagnosis or treatment target.

CC.note: Lower CYP1B1 activity; less genotoxic 4-OH-estradiol production

GG.note: ~3× higher CYP1B1 activity; more 4-OH-estradiol (genotoxic metabolite)

CG.text: Your CYP1B1 Leu432Val genotype changes enzyme activity in laboratory studies, but it does not establish that DIM or calcium D-glucarate will improve a clinical outcome.

GG.text: Your CYP1B1 Leu432Val genotype changes enzyme activity in laboratory studies; food-first cruciferous vegetables are reasonable, but this SNP does not prove a DIM or calcium D-glucarate need.

rs1501299.strandNote: Literature convention: +276 G/T. Associations vary by ancestry, diet, metabolic context, and study design; this SNP is not a standalone predictor of insulin resistance.

evidence.scope: Adiponectin, insulin-resistance, and diabetes associations vary by ancestry, diet, metabolic context, and study design.

relevance.context: Metabolic biomarkers and lived context are more informative than this genotype.

GG.note: G/G was associated with lower adiponectin and greater insulin resistance/type-2-diabetes risk in the original Italian cohort, but direction and size are not universal across populations.

GT.note: Heterozygous genotype; published associations are population- and context-dependent rather than reliably intermediate.

TT.note: T/T was the lower-risk comparison genotype in the original Italian study, while broader studies show ancestry-dependent and sometimes conflicting associations.

rs1799941.strandNote: Forward strand: G (major) / A (minor). Each A allele has been associated with higher circulating SHBG across several cohorts, but the size and downstream hormone associations vary with sex, age, body composition, and population.

evidence.scope: Several cohorts support higher circulating SHBG with the A allele, while effect size and downstream hormone relevance vary.

relevance.context: Use a measured hormone panel and personal context rather than genotype alone.

GG.note: G/G is the lower-SHBG comparison genotype in the cited cohorts.

GA.note: One A allele has been associated with higher circulating SHBG; a measured hormone panel is more informative than genotype alone.

AA.note: A/A was associated with higher SHBG than G/G, including a 39% difference in one postmenopausal cohort; that cohort-specific estimate is not a personal prediction.

rs1799945.compoundNote: Compound heterozygous with rs1800562 (CG + GA) causes moderate iron overload risk

evidence.scope: HFE H63D is well established, but penetrance is usually low unless combined with other HFE risk variants or cofactors.

relevance.context: Ferritin, transferrin saturation, the C282Y genotype, and clinical context determine relevance.

CC.note: No H63D variant

GG.note: Mild iron overload possible; significant risk if compound heterozygous with C282Y

CG.text: Your HFE H63D carrier genotype suggests checking ferritin and transferrin saturation before using iron supplements.

GG.text: Your HFE H63D genotype suggests checking ferritin and transferrin saturation and avoiding unnecessary iron supplementation.

evidence.scope: HFE C282Y is a well-established hereditary-hemochromatosis variant with strongly genotype-dependent penetrance.

relevance.context: Iron studies and professional interpretation are needed; carrier and homozygous states are not equivalent.

GG.note: No hemochromatosis risk from C282Y

GA.note: Carrier; usually asymptomatic, mildly elevated ferritin/transferrin sat possible

AA.note: Hereditary hemochromatosis (type 1); progressive iron accumulation; monitor ferritin regularly

GA.text: Your HFE C282Y carrier genotype suggests checking ferritin and transferrin saturation and avoiding iron supplementation unless deficiency is confirmed.

AA.text: Your HFE C282Y genotype warrants clinician-guided ferritin and transferrin-saturation monitoring; avoid self-directed iron supplementation unless deficiency is confirmed.

evidence.scope: A human cohort supports hepatic-lipase and lipoprotein associations but not a coronary-heart-disease difference.

relevance.context: Measured lipids and overall cardiovascular context are more useful than this SNP.

CC.note: C/C reference genotype; associated with higher hepatic-lipase activity than T-allele genotypes in the cited study

CT.note: Associated with lower hepatic-lipase activity and a different lipoprotein profile; the cited study found no coronary-heart-disease association.

TT.note: Associated with lower hepatic-lipase activity and higher HDL2 in the cited cohort, but not with reduced coronary-heart-disease risk.

rs1801131.strandNote: Minus strand gene. Forward: T(ref)/G(alt). T=A complement, G=C complement.
rs1801131.compoundNote: Compound heterozygous with rs1801133 (GA + TG) produces significant methylation impairment

evidence.scope: A1298C has a modest functional association; common-genotype health effects are small and most relevant with C677T or adverse nutrient context.

relevance.context: Homocysteine, folate, B12, and the paired MTHFR genotype determine practical relevance.

TT.note: Normal BH4 production

TG.note: Mildly reduced BH4 synthesis; homocysteine usually normal unless compound-het with C677T

GG.note: Reduced BH4; solo effect on homocysteine small in adequate-folate populations — compound-het with C677T is where clinically meaningful impairment appears

TG.text: Your MTHFR A1298C genotype has a modest effect by itself; use folate status and homocysteine rather than genotype alone to choose a folate dose or form.

GG.text: Your MTHFR A1298C genotype does not by itself establish a methylfolate need; use folate status, homocysteine, and any C677T result for context.

rs1801133.strandNote: Minus strand gene. Forward: G(ref)/A(alt). G=C complement, A=T complement.

evidence.scope: C677T has a replicated effect on MTHFR activity and homocysteine, strongly modified by folate and other nutritional context.

relevance.context: Use homocysteine and nutrient biomarkers; genotype alone does not establish disease or a supplement form.

GG.note: Normal MTHFR activity (~100%)

GA.note: ~65% enzyme activity; mild homocysteine elevation possible with low folate

AA.note: ~30% enzyme activity; likely elevated homocysteine; consider methylfolate over folic acid

GA.text: Your MTHFR C677T genotype can lower enzyme activity; use folate status and homocysteine rather than genotype alone to choose a folate dose or form.

AA.text: Your MTHFR C677T genotype can substantially lower enzyme activity, especially with low folate; labs should guide folate dosing and form.

evidence.scope: A meta-analysis supports holotranscobalamin and small homocysteine associations, primarily in European-ancestry participants.

relevance.context: Interpret with B12 biomarkers rather than diagnosing cellular deficiency from genotype.

CC.note: Associated with higher holotranscobalamin than GG in the cited meta-analysis

CG.note: Intermediate genotype; rs1801198 is associated with holotranscobalamin, but it does not by itself diagnose cellular B12 deficiency.

GG.note: Associated with lower holotranscobalamin and a small increase in homocysteine among participants of European ancestry in a meta-analysis; clinical status still requires biomarkers.

rs1801222.strandNote: Forward alleles G/A. The common A allele is associated with modestly lower circulating B12 in population studies; this association does not prove clinically important intestinal malabsorption.

evidence.scope: Population studies support a modest circulating-B12 association; this common SNP is not equivalent to rare pathogenic CUBN variants.

relevance.context: B12 biomarkers and symptoms are needed before inferring impaired status.

GG.note: Associated with higher circulating B12 than A-allele genotypes in the cited population studies

GA.note: Associated with modestly lower circulating B12; the studies do not establish a clinically important absorption defect from this genotype alone.

AA.note: Associated with lower circulating B12 in population studies. This common SNP is not equivalent to rare pathogenic CUBN variants that cause severe B12 malabsorption.

evidence.scope: Human studies support a modest insulin-sensitivity and diabetes-risk association, with population and metabolic-context limitations.

relevance.context: Body composition, diet, activity, and measured glucose control dominate personal relevance.

CC.note: Standard PPARγ2; highest insulin resistance risk

CG.note: Improved insulin sensitivity; reduced T2D risk (protective)

GG.note: Best insulin sensitivity; lowest T2D risk (protective)

evidence.scope: Common-variant effects on B12 recycling and homocysteine are modest, context-dependent, and not consistently directional across studies.

relevance.context: Homocysteine, B12, folate, riboflavin, and other variants are needed for interpretation.

AA.note: Normal B12 recycling via MTRR

GG.note: Impaired B12 recycling; can elevate homocysteine especially with low B12/riboflavin

AG.text: Your MTRR A66G genotype is an association marker; use B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, and diet before inferring a need for a particular B12 form or riboflavin.

GG.text: Your MTRR A66G genotype is an association marker; use functional B12 and homocysteine results rather than assuming methylcobalamin or riboflavin is required.

rs1805007.strandNote: Forward strand: C(ref Arg151)/T(alt Cys151). Loss-of-function for α-MSH signaling.

evidence.scope: R151C is a replicated MC1R loss-of-function pigmentation variant; UV outcomes remain phenotype- and exposure-dependent.

relevance.context: Observed skin phenotype, UV index, exposure, protection, and other pigmentation genes determine practical risk.

CC.note: Wildtype α-MSH receptor; standard tan response

CT.note: One R151C red-hair-color allele; associated with fair pigmentation and greater UV sensitivity, with phenotype modified by other pigmentation variants and sun exposure

TC.note: One R151C red-hair-color allele; associated with fair pigmentation and greater UV sensitivity, with phenotype modified by other pigmentation variants and sun exposure

TT.note: Two R151C loss-of-function alleles; strongly associated with red hair and fair, UV-sensitive pigmentation. This genotype does not support calculating an exact personal burn time.

rs1805008.strandNote: Forward strand: C(ref Arg160)/T(alt Trp160). Loss-of-function for α-MSH signaling.

evidence.scope: R160W is a replicated MC1R loss-of-function pigmentation variant; UV outcomes remain phenotype- and exposure-dependent.

relevance.context: Observed skin phenotype, UV index, exposure, protection, and other pigmentation genes determine practical risk.

CC.note: Wildtype α-MSH receptor; standard tan response

CT.note: One R160W red-hair-color allele; associated with fair pigmentation and greater UV sensitivity, with phenotype modified by other pigmentation variants and sun exposure

TC.note: One R160W red-hair-color allele; associated with fair pigmentation and greater UV sensitivity, with phenotype modified by other pigmentation variants and sun exposure

TT.note: Two R160W loss-of-function alleles; strongly associated with red hair and fair, UV-sensitive pigmentation. This genotype does not support calculating an exact personal burn time.

evidence.scope: The foundational human study did not support a homocysteine effect and described the common variant as probably benign.

relevance.context: No methylation or supplement conclusion follows from this genotype.

AA.note: Reference genotype. The foundational study did not find an association between A2756G and homocysteine concentrations.

AG.note: Heterozygous genotype. The cited study described the variant as probably benign and found no homocysteine association.

GG.note: Alternate homozygous genotype. The cited study does not support inferring reduced methionine-synthase activity or elevated homocysteine from this SNP alone.

rs2228570.strandNote: Forward strand: A/G corresponds to the literature T/C convention. A encodes the longer VDR isoform and G the shorter isoform; the cited study measured transcriptional activity in vitro, not personal vitamin D status or supplementation response.

evidence.scope: In-vitro work supports different VDR isoform activity but does not establish personal vitamin D status or treatment response.

relevance.context: Do not use this SNP to set a vitamin D target or dose.

AA.note: A/A encodes the longer VDR isoform, which had lower transcriptional activity than the shorter form in vitro. This does not establish a higher vitamin D requirement.

AG.note: A/G can produce both VDR isoforms. The functional evidence is from laboratory assays and does not predict an individual supplementation response.

GG.note: G/G encodes the shorter VDR isoform, which was more transcriptionally active in vitro; this is not a guaranteed health advantage.

rs2235321.strandNote: Forward strand: G/A. The cited studies were conducted in healthy rural Gambian adults; effects were subtle and may not generalize to other populations.

evidence.scope: Subtle hepcidin findings come from healthy rural Gambian cohorts and did not extend to broader iron-status indicators.

relevance.context: No anemia or iron-supplement conclusion follows from this marker.

GG.note: G/G had higher baseline hepcidin than A/A in the cited Gambian studies, without a significant genotype effect on other iron-status indicators.

GA.note: G/A is a common heterozygous genotype. The cited studies found subtle genotype differences in hepcidin but not in plasma iron or broader iron-status indicators.

AA.note: A/A had lower hepcidin than G/G in the cited Gambian cohorts; the studies did not establish anemia or a need for iron supplementation from this genotype.

evidence.scope: Adiponectin and insulin-resistance associations are population-stratified, stronger in some Asian cohorts and weak elsewhere.

relevance.context: Use metabolic biomarkers and ancestry context rather than this genotype alone.

TT.note: Standard adiponectin levels

TG.note: Modestly altered adiponectin; effect on insulin sensitivity is modest and mainly documented in Asian populations

GG.note: Altered adiponectin; insulin-resistance effect is population-stratified — meaningful in Asian cohorts, weak elsewhere

rs2282679.strandNote: Forward strand: T (reference) / G (alternate). The G allele is associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D and vitamin-D-binding protein in the cited GWAS; some publications report the A/C complement.

evidence.scope: Large human genetic studies consistently associate the G allele with circulating 25(OH)D and vitamin-D-binding-protein differences.

relevance.context: Measured 25(OH)D should guide interpretation and any response.

TT.note: T/T is the higher-25(OH)D comparison genotype in the cited GWAS.

GT.note: One G allele is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D and vitamin-D-binding protein; this is an association, not a personal dose requirement.

GG.note: Two G alleles are associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D and vitamin-D-binding protein. Measured 25(OH)D should guide any response.

GT.text: Your GC rs2282679 genotype is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D; use your measured level and response to personalize sun, food, or vitamin D intake.

GG.text: Your GC rs2282679 genotype is associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D; labs should guide whether your sun, food, or vitamin D intake needs adjustment.

evidence.scope: The cited human study did not demonstrate a homocysteine difference or genotype-specific folate response.

relevance.context: No BHMT impairment or supplement need should be inferred from this marker.

GG.note: Reference genotype. The cited study found no significant homocysteine difference among rs3733890 genotypes.

GA.note: Heterozygous genotype; the cited study does not support inferring reduced BHMT activity from this SNP alone.

AA.note: Alternate homozygous genotype; no significant homocysteine difference or genotype-specific folate response was demonstrated in the cited study.

evidence.scope: Human genetic evidence supports transferrin, TIBC, and transferrin-saturation associations, not a standalone iron diagnosis.

relevance.context: Interpret with ferritin, transferrin saturation, CBC, inflammation, diet, and blood loss.

GG.note: Normal transferrin/TIBC levels

AA.note: ~21% higher transferrin, ~24% higher TIBC, ~25% lower transferrin saturation

evidence.scope: UGT1A1 G71R is a well-established reduced-function variant associated with unconjugated bilirubin, especially in East Asian populations.

relevance.context: Bilirubin results, ancestry, symptoms, and medication context determine practical relevance.

GG.note: Normal UGT1A1 activity

GA.note: Mildly reduced glucuronidation; slightly elevated bilirubin

AA.note: Gilbert syndrome equivalent (common in East Asian populations); markedly elevated bilirubin

rs6013897.strandNote: Forward strand: T(ref)/A(alt). The A allele is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D; the GWAS does not establish a direct change in enzyme activity.

evidence.scope: Large human genetic studies support a modest 25(OH)D association at this locus but do not prove altered CYP24A1 activity.

relevance.context: Measured 25(OH)D is the useful check and should guide any response.

TT.note: Typical population association for circulating 25(OH)D at this locus

AT.note: One A allele is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D in population studies

TA.note: One A allele is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D in population studies

AA.note: Two A alleles are associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D; an actual vitamin D test is the useful check

AT.text: Your CYP24A1-region genotype is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D, so your measured vitamin D response may be worth watching

AA.text: Your CYP24A1-region genotype is associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D, so labs can help personalize sun, food, or vitamin D intake

evidence.scope: TCF7L2 rs7903146 is a widely replicated common type-2-diabetes association with meaningful but non-deterministic effect size.

relevance.context: Glucose markers, body composition, diet, activity, ancestry, and family history determine absolute risk.

CC.note: Normal beta cell incretin response

CT.note: ~1.5× lifetime T2D risk; mildly impaired insulin secretion. Absolute risk depends heavily on weight, diet, and activity.

TT.note: ~2× lifetime T2D risk; impaired post-prandial insulin release. Absolute risk still depends heavily on weight, diet, and activity — lifestyle matters more than genotype.

CT.text: Your TCF7L2 genotype is associated with higher type-2-diabetes risk; use glucose trends to prioritize established food, movement, sleep, and weight-management habits.

TT.text: Your TCF7L2 genotype is associated with higher type-2-diabetes risk; follow glucose trends and prioritize established lifestyle measures. The genotype alone does not establish a berberine need.

evidence.scope: The UGT1A1 TA repeat is a well-established functional bilirubin and pharmacogenetic variant with genotype-dependent effect.

relevance.context: Interpret with bilirubin, symptoms, ancestry, and medication context.

6/7.note: ~75% UGT1A1 activity; mildly elevated unconjugated bilirubin

7/7.note: Gilbert syndrome; UGT1A1 ~30-60% of normal; bilirubin 2-3× elevated; benign but affects drug metabolism

rs9939609.strandNote: dbSNP forward: T(ref, protective) / A(alt, risk). A ≈ 0.42 in Europeans, ~0.16 in East Asians, ~0.5 in Africans (weaker effect). 23andMe / Ancestry report T/A.

evidence.scope: Large cohorts and meta-analyses support a modest body-weight association that is attenuated by physical activity and varies by ancestry.

relevance.context: Diet, appetite, activity, sleep, environment, and ancestry outweigh this small population-average association.

TT.note: Lower satiety-disruption risk; standard appetite regulation

AT.note: ~+1 kg average weight effect; modest appetite-regulation impact

AA.note: The original European study reported an average weight difference of about 3 kg versus TT. A meta-analysis found that physical activity attenuated the risk-allele association with adult obesity by 27%; this is a population association, not a personal weight prediction.

rs10741657.strandNote: Forward strand: A/G. The G allele is associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D in the cited GWAS, but the marker does not by itself measure CYP2R1 enzyme activity or establish an individual dose requirement.

evidence.scope: Large human genetic studies support an association with circulating 25(OH)D but do not directly measure CYP2R1 enzyme activity.

relevance.context: Measured 25(OH)D, sun exposure, diet, and other factors determine current status.

AA.note: A/A is the higher-25(OH)D comparison genotype in the cited GWAS.

AG.note: One G allele is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D; the GWAS did not directly measure enzyme activity.

GG.note: Two G alleles are associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D; this does not by itself establish reduced hydroxylation or a supplement dose.

AG.text: Your CYP2R1 rs10741657 genotype is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D; use measured levels to personalize sun, food, or vitamin D intake.

GG.text: Your CYP2R1 rs10741657 genotype is associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D; labs should guide whether your sun, food, or vitamin D intake needs adjustment.

rs10830963.strandNote: dbSNP forward: C(ref) / G(alt = risk allele). G ≈ 0.30 globally. 23andMe / Ancestry / Illumina report C/G.

evidence.scope: Replicated human genetics and a randomized meal-timing study support glucose and late-eating interactions in G-allele carriers.

relevance.context: Meal timing, sleep timing, diet, activity, and measured glucose determine practical relevance.

CC.note: Standard fasting glucose; normal melatonin–insulin coupling

CG.note: Associated with modestly higher fasting glucose and type-2-diabetes risk. In a randomized crossover trial, glucose tolerance was worse with a meal 1 hour rather than 4 hours before habitual bedtime, especially in G-allele carriers.

GG.note: Two G risk alleles; associated with higher fasting glucose and impaired insulin secretion. A randomized crossover trial found a stronger adverse glucose response to eating 1 hour before habitual bedtime in G-allele carriers.

CG.text: Your MTNR1B genotype includes the G risk allele. In a randomized crossover trial, eating 1 hour rather than 4 hours before habitual bedtime worsened glucose tolerance, especially in G-allele carriers.

GG.text: Your MTNR1B genotype has two G risk alleles. The cited randomized crossover trial supports avoiding meals very close to bedtime, but it does not establish a guaranteed HbA1c effect.

rs10877012.strandNote: Forward G/T corresponds to literature C/A. In the cited functional study, the literature C allele (forward G) had lower promoter activity than A (forward T); results came from an elderly cohort and an in-vitro reporter assay.

evidence.scope: Promoter-reporter experiments support allele-specific activity, while the human cohort did not show a consistent serum 25(OH)D difference.

relevance.context: Do not infer active-vitamin-D production or supplementation needs from this SNP.

GG.note: Forward G/G (literature C/C) had lower promoter activity than A-containing constructs in vitro. The study did not find a consistent genotype difference in serum 25(OH)D.

GT.note: Forward G/T (literature C/A); promoter activity differed by allele in vitro, but this common SNP does not directly measure active-vitamin-D production in an individual.

TT.note: Forward T/T (literature A/A) had higher promoter-reporter activity than C/C in vitro. It should not be interpreted as guaranteed compensation for low 25(OH)D.

evidence.scope: A small study reported a reverse-T3 association but no T3, T4, or levothyroxine-response difference.

relevance.context: No genotype-specific thyroid treatment follows from this preliminary marker.

CC.note: Reference genotype in the cited study of women with hypothyroidism; rs11206244 was not associated with T3, T4, or levothyroxine response.

CT.note: Heterozygous genotype. The small cited study linked the T allele to higher reverse T3, but not to T3, T4, or levothyroxine response.

TT.note: T/T genotype. In a small study, the T allele was associated with higher reverse T3 but not lower T3/T4 or a different levothyroxine response; no genotype-specific treatment follows from it.

evidence.scope: PCSK9 R46L is a replicated loss-of-function variant associated with lower LDL and lower ischemic-heart-disease risk.

relevance.context: A measured lipid panel remains necessary; this protective association does not cancel other risk factors.

GG.note: Normal PCSK9 function

GT.note: PCSK9 loss-of-function carrier; associated with roughly 11–16% lower LDL, lower lipoprotein(a), and lower ischemic-heart-disease risk in population studies

TT.note: Very rare; very low LDL; strong protective effect

rs12785878.strandNote: Forward strand: T (reference) / G (alternate). The G allele is associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D, but this locus marker does not by itself establish DHCR7 expression or the amount of skin precursor available.

evidence.scope: Large human genetic studies support a circulating-25(OH)D association at the NADSYN1/DHCR7 locus without proving the proposed mechanism.

relevance.context: Measured 25(OH)D should guide interpretation and any response.

TT.note: T/T is the higher-25(OH)D comparison genotype in the cited GWAS.

TG.note: One G allele is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D; the mechanism and personal effect size are not established by this marker.

GT.note: One G allele is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D; the mechanism and personal effect size are not established by this marker.

GG.note: Two G alleles are associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D; this does not directly prove higher DHCR7 expression or a supplement need.

GT.text: Your NADSYN1/DHCR7-locus genotype is associated with modestly lower circulating 25(OH)D; use measured levels to evaluate your sun, food, or vitamin D response.

GG.text: Your NADSYN1/DHCR7-locus genotype is associated with lower circulating 25(OH)D; labs should guide whether your sun, food, or vitamin D intake needs adjustment.

rs4680.strandNote: Forward strand: G(ref Val) / A(alt Met). This functional variant changes COMT activity, but does not determine personality, mood, or treatment response by itself.

evidence.scope: Val158Met has a replicated effect on COMT enzyme activity; personality, cognition, and treatment claims are not included.

relevance.context: This is biochemical context, not a mental-health prediction or supplement indication.

GG.note: Val/Val; higher COMT enzyme activity and faster catecholamine breakdown than Met carriers. This is a biochemical trait, not a standalone prediction of stress response or behavior.

AG.note: Val/Met; intermediate COMT activity. Effects on cognition and stress-related traits are small, context-dependent, and inconsistent across studies.

AA.note: Met/Met; lower COMT activity and slower catecholamine breakdown than Val carriers. This does not by itself establish a mental-health or supplement need.

rs1815739.strandNote: Forward strand: C(ref R577) / T(alt X577 stop). Athletic-performance associations are population- and sport-dependent and are not training prescriptions.

evidence.scope: ACTN3 deficiency is a well-established functional trait; performance enrichment is modest, population-dependent, and non-deterministic.

relevance.context: The genotype does not prescribe a sport or training style.

CC.note: R/R; alpha-actinin-3 is expressed in fast-twitch muscle fibers. The genotype is modestly enriched in some sprint/power cohorts but does not determine performance.

CT.note: R/X; one functional ACTN3 copy. This common genotype is compatible with the full range of athletic abilities.

TT.note: X/X; alpha-actinin-3 deficiency, a common healthy muscle phenotype. Any endurance association is modest and is not a reason to avoid power training.

rs4988235.strandNote: Forward genomic strand: G(ref, corresponding to −13910C) / A(alt, corresponding to −13910T). Strongly informative in European-ancestry populations; other populations have additional lactase-persistence variants.

evidence.scope: This enhancer is strongly predictive of lactase persistence in many European-ancestry populations, with different causal variants elsewhere.

relevance.context: Ancestry, symptoms, dairy type, amount, and food matrix determine lived tolerance.

GG.note: Associated with adult lactase non-persistence in many European-ancestry populations. It predicts enzyme persistence, not whether dairy actually causes symptoms; ancestry and the food matrix matter.

AG.note: One lactase-persistence allele; usually associated with continued adult lactase expression in populations where this variant is informative.

AA.note: Two lactase-persistence alleles; usually associated with continued adult lactase expression in populations where this variant is informative.

rs1229984.strandNote: Forward genomic strand: C(ref Arg48) / T(alt His48). The His allele accelerates ethanol oxidation; frequency and effect estimates vary substantially by ancestry.

evidence.scope: ADH1B His48 has a replicated functional effect and population association with lower alcohol consumption and dependence risk.

relevance.context: Ancestry and alcohol exposure matter, and the allele does not make drinking harmless.

CC.note: Arg/Arg; slower ADH1B ethanol oxidation relative to His48 carriers. This does not imply that alcohol is safe or beneficial.

CT.note: Arg/His; faster initial ethanol oxidation and, across many populations, lower average alcohol consumption and alcohol-dependence risk. It does not remove alcohol-related health risks.

TT.note: His/His; markedly faster initial ethanol oxidation and lower alcohol-dependence risk in population studies. It does not make drinking harmless.

rs12934922.strandNote: Forward strand: A(ref Arg267) / T(alt Ser267). This affects provitamin-A carotenoid conversion, not absorption of preformed vitamin A.

evidence.scope: Human conversion studies support reduced provitamin-A carotenoid conversion, especially as part of the wider BCO1 haplotype.

relevance.context: Diet, the paired BCO1 variant, and measured nutritional context determine practical relevance.

AA.note: Arg/Arg at BCO1 R267S; no reduced-conversion allele at this site. Other BCO1 variants and dietary factors still affect beta-carotene conversion.

AT.note: One Ser267 allele; associated with less efficient beta-carotene conversion, especially when combined with rs7501331. Vitamin A status is better assessed from diet and appropriate labs than genotype alone.

TT.note: Two Ser267 alleles; associated with less efficient beta-carotene conversion. This does not automatically indicate deficiency or justify high-dose preformed vitamin A.

rs7501331.strandNote: Forward strand: C(ref Ala379) / T(alt Val379). Combined BCO1 variants can have a larger effect than this marker alone.

evidence.scope: Human conversion studies support reduced provitamin-A carotenoid conversion, with combined BCO1 variants producing larger effects.

relevance.context: Diet, the paired BCO1 variant, and measured nutritional context determine practical relevance.

CC.note: Ala/Ala at BCO1 A379V; no reduced-conversion allele at this site. Other variants and dietary factors can still influence carotenoid conversion.

CT.note: Ala/Val; associated with reduced beta-carotene conversion. The practical effect depends on the rest of the BCO1 haplotype and diet.

TT.note: Val/Val; associated with reduced beta-carotene conversion. This does not by itself diagnose vitamin A deficiency or establish a supplement dose.

rs12913832.strandNote: Forward strand: A(ref) / G(alt). Eye-color prediction is strongest in European-ancestry populations and is modified by several other pigmentation genes.

evidence.scope: This HERC2/OCA2 regulatory marker is strongly associated with eye pigmentation in European-ancestry prediction models.

relevance.context: This is a pigmentation trait modified by ancestry and other genes, with no health action implied.

AA.note: More often associated with brown or darker eye pigmentation in European-ancestry prediction models; other pigmentation variants can change the observed color.

AG.note: Intermediate pigmentation tendency; hazel, green, or brown eyes are common outcomes depending on other pigmentation variants.

GG.note: Strongly associated with blue or lighter eye pigmentation in European-ancestry prediction models, with modification by other genes.

rs10455872.strandNote: Forward strand: A(ref) / G(alt risk allele). This variant is most informative in European-ancestry populations and does not capture all genetic causes of high Lp(a).

evidence.scope: Replicated human studies link the G allele to higher Lp(a) and coronary risk, especially in European-ancestry populations.

relevance.context: A direct Lp(a) measurement is needed because this marker does not capture all genetic causes or the actual level.

AA.note: No rs10455872 Lp(a)-raising allele detected. This does not rule out elevated Lp(a); a direct Lp(a) measurement remains the relevant check.

AG.note: One Lp(a)-raising allele; associated with higher Lp(a) and increased coronary risk. Confirm with a direct Lp(a) blood measurement because genotype does not determine the exact level.

GG.note: Two Lp(a)-raising alleles, a rare genotype associated with substantially higher Lp(a). A direct Lp(a) blood measurement is needed to determine the actual level.

rs3798220.strandNote: Forward strand: T(ref Ile) / C(alt Met risk allele). Allele frequency differs greatly by ancestry, and absence does not rule out high Lp(a).

evidence.scope: Replicated human studies link Met1891 to higher Lp(a) and coronary risk, with substantial ancestry-frequency differences.

relevance.context: A direct Lp(a) measurement is needed because absence does not exclude high Lp(a) and genotype does not give the actual level.

TT.note: No rs3798220 Lp(a)-raising allele detected. Other LPA variants can still produce high Lp(a), so this is not a substitute for measurement.

CT.note: One Met1891 allele; associated with higher Lp(a) and increased coronary risk. Confirm with a direct Lp(a) blood measurement.

CC.note: Two Met1891 alleles, an exceptionally rare genotype associated with high Lp(a). A direct Lp(a) blood measurement is needed for the actual level.
